title: What is Programming
summary: Understand what code is and write your very first Python program.
definition: Programming means writing step-by-step instructions that a computer follows. Python is a readable language used by beginners and professionals. The goal is not to memorize syntax first, but to understand how instructions, values, and order work together.
howItWorks: print() is a function that shows text on the screen.
Text goes inside quotes so Python knows it is a string of characters.
Python runs your lines from top to bottom, one at a time.
Think of a program as a recipe: each instruction changes the computer's current state, and the order matters.
fullExample:
# A program is a list of instructions
print("Welcome to PyPath")
print("Computers follow instructions in order")
print("This line runs third")
practiceTask: Change the program so it prints your name on one line and something you want to build with Python on the next line.
starterCode:
# Print two lines about yourself
print("Hello!")

title: Variables
summary: Store and reuse information with named variables.
definition: A variable is a name that stores a value so you can use it later. This simple idea becomes the foundation for storing input, calculations, results, and program state.
howItWorks: The = sign stores the value on the right under the name on the left.
You can change a variable by assigning a new value to the same name.
Use clear lowercase names, with underscores between words, such as player_score.
Choose descriptive variable names because readable names make larger programs easier to understand and debug.
fullExample:
name = "Sam"
score = 10
print(name, "has", score, "points")

score = score + 5
print(name, "now has", score, "points")
practiceTask: Create one variable for your favourite colour and one for a number. Print a sentence that uses both.
starterCode:
# Create your variables here
colour = "blue"
number = 7
print(colour, number)

title: Data Types
summary: Meet strings, integers, floats and booleans, the building blocks of data.
definition: Every value has a type. The most common types are str (text), int (whole numbers), float (decimal numbers) and bool (True or False). Knowing the type of a value helps you predict what operations will work and how Python will treat it.
howItWorks: type() tells you what kind of value you have.
Whole numbers are int, numbers with a decimal point are float.
True and False are bool values and are written with a capital letter.
Python can convert between compatible types, but conversions can fail when the text does not represent the requested type.
fullExample:
text = "Python"
count = 3
price = 2.5
is_fun = True

for value in [text, count, price, is_fun]:
    print(value, "is a", type(value).__name__)

print(int("12") + 1)
print(str(12) + "1")
practiceTask: Make one value of each type (str, int, float, bool) and print its type. Then convert the string "8" to an int and add 2.
starterCode:
word = "hello"
print(type(word))

title: Input and Output
summary: Talk to the user with print() and input().
definition: print() shows information to the user. input() asks the user to type something. input() always gives you text. Input and output are the basic connection between a program and the person using it.
howItWorks: input() shows its question, then waits for a line of text.
The answer is a string, so use int() or float() when you need a number.
In PyPath, type one answer per line in the Input box under the console before you press Run.
When input is used in a calculation, convert it first because input() returns a string rather than a number.
fullExample:
name = input("What is your name? ")
age = int(input("How old are you? "))

print("Hi", name)
print("Next year you will be", age + 1)
practiceTask: Ask for the user's favourite food and print a sentence that uses the answer. Add your answer in the Input box.
starterCode:
food = input("Favourite food? ")
print("You like", food)

title: Operators
summary: Do maths and comparisons with Python's operators.
definition: Operators are symbols that work on values: arithmetic (+ - * /), comparison (== != < >) and logic (and, or, not). Learning these operators gives you the building blocks for calculations and decisions.
howItWorks: Arithmetic operators return numbers: // is whole-number division, % is the remainder and ** is the power.
Comparison operators return True or False.
and, or and not combine True/False answers.
Operator precedence follows familiar maths rules, but parentheses are useful when you want the intended order to be obvious.
fullExample:
a = 17
b = 5

print(a + b, a - b, a * b)
print(a / b, a // b, a % b, a ** 2)

print(a > b, a == b, a != b)
print(a > 10 and b < 3)
print(a > 10 or b < 3)
print(not a > 10)
practiceTask: Calculate the area of a rectangle that is 8 wide and 5 high, then print whether the area is greater than 30.
starterCode:
width = 8
height = 5
print(width * height)

title: Conditions
summary: Make decisions in code with if, elif and else.
definition: Conditions let your program choose what to do. Python uses if, elif and else. Once conditions are clear, programs can respond differently to different data instead of following one fixed path.
howItWorks: The line with if ends with a colon.
The indented lines belong to that if and only run when the condition is True.
elif checks another condition, and else runs when nothing above matched.
Keep conditions focused on one decision at a time; this makes branches easier to test and avoids deeply nested code.
practiceTask: Write a program that stores a score from 0 to 100 and prints A for 90 or more, B for 80 or more, C for 70 or more, otherwise Try again.
starterCode:
score = 85
# Add if / elif / else here
print(score)

title: Loops
summary: Repeat work automatically with for and while loops.
definition: A loop repeats instructions. A for loop repeats over a sequence, and a while loop repeats while a condition is True. Repetition is what lets a small amount of code handle many values or repeated actions.
howItWorks: range(3) gives 0, 1, 2.
A while loop checks its condition before every repeat, so something inside must change or it never stops.
break leaves a loop early and continue skips to the next repeat.
Choose for when you know what collection or range you want to visit, and while when repetition depends on a changing condition.
fullExample:
for number in range(1, 6):
    print("Number", number)

countdown = 3
while countdown > 0:
    print(countdown)
    countdown = countdown - 1
print("Liftoff")
practiceTask: Use a for loop to print the 5 times table from 5 x 1 up to 5 x 10.
starterCode:
for i in range(1, 11):
    print(i)

title: Loop Control: break and continue
summary: Take control of loops with break, continue and loop else.
definition: break stops a loop immediately, continue skips to the next round, and a loop's else block runs only when the loop was not stopped by break. These controls give you precise control over when a loop continues and when it stops.
howItWorks: break leaves the loop as soon as it runs, so this example prints 1 to 4 only.
continue jumps straight to the next round and skips the rest of the loop body.
A loop's else block runs only if the loop finished without hitting break.
Use break and continue deliberately because they change the normal flow of a loop and can make debugging harder if overused.
practiceTask: Change 21 to 22 in the list and run again. Which message appears now, and why?
starterCode:
numbers = [4, 9, 14, 17, 22, 25]

# TODO: loop over numbers, skip multiples of 2 with continue,
# and stop with break at the first number bigger than 15
for n in numbers:
    print(n)

title: Functions
summary: Package reusable logic into your own functions.
definition: A function is a named block of code you can reuse. Functions take inputs (parameters) and can give back a result with return. Functions are one of the main tools for turning repeated ideas into reusable building blocks.
howItWorks: def starts the function and the indented lines are its body.
Parameters are the names for the values you pass in.
return sends a value back to the code that called the function.
A good function usually has one clear job, which makes it easier to test, reuse, and combine with other functions.
fullExample:
def greet(name):
    return "Hello, " + name + "!"

def add(a, b=0):
    return a + b

print(greet("Ada"))
print(add(2, 3))
print(add(10))
practiceTask: Write a function square(n) that returns n times n, then print square(4) and square(9).

title: Lists
summary: Keep ordered collections of values in lists.
definition: A list stores many values in order. Lists are written with square brackets and can be changed. They are one of Python's most important tools for working with collections of data.
howItWorks: Positions start at 0, so fruits[0] is the first item and fruits[-1] is the last.
append() adds an item, remove() deletes one and len() counts the items.
A for loop can visit every item in a list.
Lists are mutable, so changing a list affects the same list object; use a copy when you need an independent collection.
fullExample:
scores = [70, 85, 90]
scores.append(100)

print(scores)
print("First:", scores[0], "Last:", scores[-1])
print("Count:", len(scores))
print("Total:", sum(scores))

for s in sorted(scores, reverse=True):
    print(s)
practiceTask: Make a list of five of your favourite things. Add one more item, then print each item on its own line.
starterCode:
things = ["music", "football"]
print(things)

title: Dictionaries
summary: Look up values by key with dictionaries.
definition: A dictionary stores data as key and value pairs, so you can look things up by name instead of position. This makes dictionaries especially useful for records, configuration, lookups, and structured information.
howItWorks: Keys inside the curly braces are joined to values with a colon.
dict[key] reads a value and dict[key] = value adds or changes one.
get() returns a default instead of an error when a key is missing.
Dictionary keys should be stable and unique, while values can be almost any useful Python object.
fullExample:
student = {"name": "Ada", "age": 12}
student["grade"] = "A"
student["age"] = 13

print(student["name"])
print(student.get("city", "unknown"))

for key, value in student.items():
    print(key, "->", value)
practiceTask: Create a dictionary for a book with title, author and year. Print each pair on its own line.
starterCode:
book = {"title": "My Book"}
print(book)

title: Tuples and Sets
summary: Use immutable tuples and duplicate-free sets.
definition: A tuple is an ordered group that cannot be changed. A set is a collection of unique items with no order. Understanding the difference helps you choose the right collection for the problem you are solving.
howItWorks: Tuples use round brackets and are good for fixed groups such as coordinates.
Sets remove duplicates automatically.
Sets support union (|), intersection (&) and difference (-).
Use a tuple for fixed grouped data and a set when uniqueness or fast membership checks matter more than ordering.
fullExample:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print("x =", x, "y =", y)

a = {1, 2, 3, 3}
b = {3, 4}
print(a)
print(a | b)
print(a & b)
print(a - b)
print(3 in a)
practiceTask: Remove the duplicates from the list [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3] by turning it into a set, then print how many unique numbers there are.
starterCode:
numbers = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]
print(numbers)

title: String Methods
summary: Clean, search and reshape text with string methods.
definition: Strings have built-in methods for changing, searching and splitting text. String methods are especially useful when cleaning and preparing user input.
howItWorks: Methods are called with a dot, like text.upper().
Strings cannot be changed, so each method returns a new string.
split() breaks text into a list and join() joins a list into text.
String methods return new strings because Python strings cannot be changed in place.
fullExample:
text = "  Learn Python Step By Step  "
clean = text.strip()

print(clean.upper())
print(clean.lower())
print(clean.replace("Step", "Small step"))
print(clean.startswith("Learn"))

words = clean.split(" ")
print(words)
print("-".join(words))
print(f"The text has {len(words)} words")
practiceTask: Take the sentence "python is fun", capitalise each word and print it. Hint: split, title or capitalize, then join.
starterCode:
sentence = "python is fun"
print(sentence)

title: File Handling
summary: Read and write files so data outlives your program.
definition: Programs can write text to files and read it back. The with statement closes the file for you. File handling lets a program keep information after it finishes running.
howItWorks: Mode "w" writes (and replaces the file), "a" appends and "r" reads.
with closes the file automatically, even if there is an error.
In PyPath the files live in temporary browser memory and disappear when you refresh.
Use with open(...) so files are closed reliably even when an error occurs while reading or writing.
fullExample:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Line one\n")
    f.write("Line two\n")

with open("notes.txt", "r") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())

import os
print(os.path.exists("notes.txt"))
os.remove("notes.txt")
print(os.path.exists("notes.txt"))
practiceTask: Write three names to a file called names.txt, then read the file and print how many lines it has.
starterCode:
with open("names.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Ada\n")

with open("names.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())

title: Error Handling
summary: Handle problems gracefully with try and except.
definition: Errors happen. try and except let your program deal with them instead of stopping. Handling errors well makes programs more reliable and gives users clearer feedback.
howItWorks: Code that might fail goes in the try block.
except runs only if that kind of error happens.
finally always runs, which is useful for tidy-up work.
Catch specific exceptions when possible so genuine programming mistakes are not hidden by a broad except block.
practiceTask: Write a function to_number(text) that returns an int, or 0 if the text is not a number. Test it with "5" and "five".

title: Modules and Imports
summary: Reuse code from Python's standard library and your own modules.
definition: A module is a file of ready-made Python code. import lets you use it, and the standard library has many useful modules. The standard library gives Python a large set of tested tools without requiring you to build everything yourself.
howItWorks: import brings in a whole module and you call things as module.name.
from module import name brings in just one name.
Popular modules include math, random, datetime, json and statistics.
Imports keep programs modular: put reusable code in modules and import only what the current program needs.
fullExample:
import math
import statistics
from random import randint, seed

print(math.sqrt(49), math.pi)
print(math.ceil(4.2), math.floor(4.8))

marks = [60, 70, 80, 90]
print(statistics.mean(marks))
print(statistics.median(marks))

seed(1)
print(randint(1, 100))
practiceTask: Use the math module to print the circumference of a circle with radius 5 (2 * pi * r).
starterCode:
import math
print(math.pi)

title: Function Arguments
summary: Write flexible functions with defaults, *args and **kwargs.
definition: Functions can have default values, keyword arguments, *args for any number of positional values and **kwargs for any number of named values. These features let one function stay convenient for simple calls while still supporting more advanced use cases.
howItWorks: A default value is used when the caller leaves that argument out.
*args collects extra positional values into a tuple.
**kwargs collects extra named values into a dictionary.
Keyword arguments make calls easier to read, while *args and **kwargs are useful when a function needs flexible inputs.
practiceTask: Write a function average(*numbers) that returns the average of any amount of numbers. Call it with two, three and five numbers.

    pass

print(average(1, 2, 3))

title: Classes and Objects
summary: Model real things with classes and objects.
definition: A class is a blueprint. An object is one thing built from that blueprint, with its own data and actions. This is the foundation of object-oriented programming in Python.
howItWorks: __init__ runs when a new object is created and sets its starting data.
self is the object itself, and self.name is data stored on it.
Functions inside a class are called methods.
Objects combine state and behaviour, which helps model real things when several values and operations belong together.
practiceTask: Create a class Rectangle with width and height and a method area() that returns the area. Make two rectangles and print both areas.

title: Inheritance
summary: Build new classes on top of existing ones with inheritance.
definition: Inheritance lets a new class reuse and extend another class. The new class is the child and the original is the parent. Used carefully, inheritance can remove repeated code while keeping related classes consistent.
howItWorks: Put the parent class name in brackets after the child name.
The child gets every method of the parent automatically.
A child can override a method, and super() reaches the parent version.
Inheritance is useful when classes share a genuine relationship; composition is often simpler when the relationship is about using another object.
practiceTask: Add a Bird class that inherits from Animal and overrides speak() to say Tweet. Create a bird and print what it says.

title: List Comprehensions
summary: Create lists in a single expressive line.
definition: A list comprehension builds a new list in one short line. This combines a loop and an expression into a compact way to create a new list.
codeExample: squares = [n * n for n in range(5)]
howItWorks: The pattern is [expression for item in sequence].
Add if at the end to keep only some items.
If the loop body gets complicated, use a normal for loop instead.
Comprehensions are best when the transformation is simple enough to remain readable; use a normal loop for more complicated logic.
fullExample:
numbers = list(range(1, 11))

squares = [n * n for n in numbers]
evens = [n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]
words = [w.upper() for w in ["red", "green", "blue"]]

print(squares)
print(evens)
print(words)
practiceTask: Use a list comprehension to make a list of the cubes (n * n * n) of the odd numbers from 1 to 9.
starterCode:
odds = [n for n in range(1, 10) if n % 2 == 1]
print(odds)

title: Lambda Functions
summary: Write tiny anonymous functions with lambda.
definition: A lambda is a tiny nameless function written on one line. It is often used with sorted, map and filter. It is powerful for small transformations, especially when used with collection functions.
howItWorks: lambda arguments: expression returns the expression's value.
sorted(items, key=...) sorts using the value your lambda returns.
map transforms every item and filter keeps items that pass a test.
A lambda is useful for a short one-off function, but a named def is clearer when the logic needs explanation or reuse.
fullExample:
people = [("Ada", 30), ("Bo", 25), ("Cy", 35)]

print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1]))

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
print(list(map(lambda n: n * 10, numbers)))
print(list(filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, numbers)))
practiceTask: Sort the list of words ["pear", "fig", "banana"] by length using a lambda.
starterCode:
words = ["pear", "fig", "banana"]
print(sorted(words))

title: Generators and Iterators
summary: Produce values one at a time with iterators and generators.
definition: A generator makes values one at a time with yield, instead of building a whole list in memory. This is important when working with streams, large files, or calculations that would otherwise use lots of memory.
howItWorks: yield pauses the function and hands back one value.
The function continues from the same place when the next value is asked for.
Generators are ideal for long or endless sequences.
Generators are lazy, so they can process large sequences without storing every result in memory at once.
practiceTask: Write a generator evens(limit) that yields the even numbers from 2 up to limit. Print the values for limit = 12.

title: Decorators
summary: Wrap functions with extra behaviour using decorators.
definition: A decorator wraps a function to add behaviour before or after it runs, without changing the function itself. They are a practical example of higher-order functions because functions can be passed around and returned.
howItWorks: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new one.
The @ line is a short way to write hello = my_decorator(hello).
The wrapper uses *args and **kwargs so it works with any function.
Decorators receive a function and return a wrapped function, making them useful for reusable logging, timing, validation, and access checks.
practiceTask: Write a decorator called twice that runs the function two times. Use it on a function that prints Hello.

title: Working with APIs
summary: Understand how programs talk to web services and read JSON.
definition: An API is a way for programs to ask other programs for data. Most web APIs reply with JSON, which Python turns into dictionaries and lists. Learning to work with APIs connects Python programs to real services and external information.
howItWorks: json.loads() converts JSON text into Python dictionaries and lists.
urllib.parse builds safe request URLs from parts.
PyPath does not send network requests from your code, so this lesson uses a sample reply that works offline.
APIs have contracts: read the endpoint, parameters, response shape, and error behavior before relying on external data.
fullExample:
import json
from urllib.parse import urlencode

url = "https://api.example.com/weather?" + urlencode({"city": "Sample City", "units": "metric"})
print("Request:", url)

reply = '{"city": "Sample City", "temp": 31.5, "conditions": ["sunny", "humid"]}'
data = json.loads(reply)

print(data["city"], "is", data["temp"], "degrees")
for item in data["conditions"]:
    print("-", item)

print(json.dumps(data, indent=2))
practiceTask: Parse this sample reply: {"user": "ada", "repos": 12}. Print a sentence that says how many repositories the user has.
starterCode:

reply = '{"user": "ada", "repos": 12}'
data = json.loads(reply)
print(data)

title: Type Hints, Docstrings and Testing
summary: Write clearer, safer code with type hints, docstrings and tests.
definition: Good Python code explains itself with type hints and docstrings, and proves it works with small tests written using assert. These practices move code from simply working once to being easier to maintain safely.
codeExample:
def double(n: int) -> int:
    """Return n multiplied by two."""
    return n * 2

assert double(4) == 8
howItWorks: Type hints (n: int, -> int) document what a function expects and returns.
A docstring in triple quotes describes what the function does.
assert raises an error when a condition is false, so a test fails loudly instead of silently.
Tests should cover normal cases, edge cases, and failure cases so changes can be made with confidence.
fullExample:
def is_palindrome(text: str) -> bool:
    """Return True if text reads the same forwards and backwards."""
    cleaned = "".join(ch.lower() for ch in text if ch.isalnum())
    return cleaned == cleaned[::-1]

def test_is_palindrome() -> None:
    assert is_palindrome("level")
    assert is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")
    assert not is_palindrome("python")
    print("All tests passed")

test_is_palindrome()
print(is_palindrome.__doc__)

title: Project 1: Calculator

definition: A calculator project combines input, functions and conditions to solve a practical problem. The project combines several earlier skills into one small program with a clear input-to-result flow.
codeExample:

    return a + b
howItWorks: Each operation lives in its own small function.
input() collects two numbers and an operator.
if / elif chooses the right function, and a check stops division by zero.
A useful calculator separates input, validation, calculation, and output so each part can be changed without rewriting the whole program.

title: Project 2: Guess the Number
summary: Project 2: Build a higher-or-lower number guessing game.
definition: A guessing game uses the random module, a while loop and conditions to compare the player's guess with a secret number. The project turns conditions, loops, input, and random values into an interactive program.
howItWorks: random.randint(1, 10) picks a whole number from 1 to 10.
The while loop repeats until the guess is right or the attempts run out.
if / elif / else tells the player whether to go higher or lower.
A guessing game teaches state and repetition: the secret stays fixed while each guess updates the number of attempts.
fullExample:
import random

secret = random.randint(1, 10)
attempts = 0
guess = 0

print("I am thinking of a number from 1 to 10.")
while guess != secret and attempts < 10:
    guess = int(input("Your guess: "))
    attempts = attempts + 1
    if guess < secret:
        print("Too low")
    elif guess > secret:
        print("Too high")
    else:
        print("Correct! You needed", attempts, "guesses.")
practiceTask: Change the range to 1-50 and update the guesses in the Input box. Then add a message that tells the player how many guesses are left.

strip() and lower() make the answer check forgiving, and a score counter is shown at the end.
A quiz becomes easier to extend when questions are stored as data instead of being hard-coded into separate blocks of logic.

title: Project 4: Expense Tracker

A Tracker class keeps a list of expenses and offers methods such as add() and total().
